planting.note: Set out container plants in fall or early spring in a sheltered spot with sharp drainage; this Balearic native is markedly less cold-hardy than the common Lenten rose and benefits from a warm wall or dry-shade position.

directions: Grow in gritty, sharply drained soil in dappled or partial shade, since this species resents winter wet far more than mainstream Lenten rose hybrids. The leathery, three-part leaves are heavily marbled with silver-grey veining and stay attractive year-round, while dusky pink-flushed pale green flowers open in late winter atop reddish stems. Because it originates from the Balearic Islands it is noticeably tender, so gardeners outside its comfortable range often grow it against a warm wall or in a container that can be moved under cover for hard freezes. It is a parent species of many marbled-leaf hybrids such as Helleborus x sternii, and all plant parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in open woodland shade; this small Balkan species is slower to establish than garden hybrids but is prized by breeders for its intense dark flower color.

directions: Site in humus-rich, free-draining soil in partial to full shade, ideally at the base of deciduous shrubs where summer moisture is retained but winter drainage stays sharp. This compact species from the western Balkans carries small, nodding flowers ranging from smoky purple to near-black, often with a contrasting silvery or green reverse, and finely dissected foliage that dies back in summer heat. It has long been used by specialist breeders to deepen and darken the color range of garden Lenten rose hybrids, so true species plants are less common in trade than its offspring. Give it a cool root run and leave the previous year's leaves in place until new growth begins, since the crown is more cold-sensitive when bare; all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in fall in cool, moisture-retentive woodland soil high in leaf mold; this Chinese species is unusual among hellebores in going fully dormant and losing its leaves in summer.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in cool woodland shade, replicating the mountain forest conditions of its native Hubei and Sichuan provinces. Nodding, bell-shaped flowers in shades of pale pink to rose, often flushed or veined with deeper pink, appear on bare stems before the pleated foliage emerges in early spring. Unlike most garden hellebores it dies back completely by midsummer and re-emerges the following late winter, so mark its location and interplant with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap. It resents summer waterlogging and hot, humid climates, making it best suited to cooler temperate gardens with reliable winter chill; all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Potter's Wheel Hellebore (Large-Flowered White Christmas Rose)

planting.note: Plant in fall in neutral to alkaline, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this RHS Award of Garden Merit selection is grown for exceptionally large, flat-faced white flowers.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade, working in compost or well-rotted manure at planting time since Christmas rose selections are heavier feeders than most Lenten rose hybrids. Potter's Wheel produces some of the largest flowers in the species, wide and flat-faced in pure white with a prominent central boss of golden stamens and faint green veining near the eye, held above dark, leathery evergreen foliage from midwinter into early spring. It is a long-lived, slow-to-establish clone best left undisturbed once planted rather than divided frequently, and it benefits from a light mulch and shelter from harsh winter wind to protect the earliest buds. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Ashwood Garden Hybrids Hellebore (Ashwood Strain Lenten Rose)

planting.note: Plant fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ashwood Garden Hybrids are a hand-pollinated strain bred by England's Ashwood Nurseries for exceptional form, substance, and color range.

directions: Grow in rich, humus-amended, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching annually with leaf mold or compost to sustain the vigorous growth this strain is known for. Ashwood Garden Hybrids trace to decades of selective hand-pollination by Kevin Belcher at Ashwood Nurseries in England, prized for rounded overlapping petals, heavy substance, outward or upward-facing flowers, and a color range spanning slate, anemone-centered doubles, picotees, and richly spotted forms. Because the strain is seed-raised rather than a single clone, expect variation between plants, and remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before flowering to best display the blooms. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
